prime.problem: Lecture 1 teaches backprop in Python that quietly relies on dunder methods, closures and recursion. If 2*a, out._backward or build_topo look like magic, you spend the lecture decoding syntax instead of following the math.
prime.fits: This is the first card of the series and needs nothing before it except basic Python (functions, classes, lists, loops). Every later micrograd card, starting with the Value object, is built from the five features here.
prime.goal: Predict exactly which method Python calls for a*b, 2*a and sum(...), write a small class that supports all three, and explain why micrograd stores a function in out._backward and why build_topo needs visited.

attend: Python tries the left operand first. What does int answer when it meets a Money, and what does Python do with that answer?
Why does sum([m1, m2]) need __radd__ even though you never write a number on the left yourself?
When __mul__ has already returned, how can the _backward it defined still reach self, other and out?
What single rule does build_topo follow that guarantees every node lands after all of its inputs?
Which job does the visited set do that the recursion alone can't?

must: x * y first calls x.__mul__(y) → a plain int doesn't know your class and returns NotImplemented → Python then tries y.__rmul__(x) → without it 2*a is a TypeError, and sum() (which starts from 0) fails the same way without __radd__

Operators are method calls → the method creates the result object itself → it can attach anything to that result (micrograd: the parents, the op and a backward function) → ordinary-looking formulas build the graph
A function defined inside a method captures that call's variables → it can be stored on the result and called much later → each result carries its own local-derivative code for backprop to run

build_topo appends a node only after recursing into all its inputs → every node sits after its inputs → reversed, every node's gradient is complete before its _backward runs; the visited set stops a shared node running twice (without it, a.grad comes out 96 or 102 instead of 66 in the Predict step)
elevated: Recursion depth is capped (1,000 frames by default in Python 3.10.14) → micrograd's recursive build_topo handles a chain of 995 additions and raises RecursionError at 996 → fine for the lecture's nets, but deep graphs need an explicit stack
reference: the exact __repr__ format string and f-string syntax
the isinstance(other, Money) else Money(other) wrapping line (copy it)
zip and the start argument of sum(iterable, start)
nested comprehension order: [p for layer in layers for p in layer.parameters()]
lambda i=i: i as the fix for closures made in a loop

compress.prompt: From memory, in 3–5 sentences, explain what Python does when it runs 3 * m1, and how micrograd uses a closure and a set to run backprop in the right order. Or draw the call sequence for 3 * m1 and the build_topo order for L = d·f, d = e + c, e = a·b.
checklist: operators are dunder-method calls on the left operand first
NotImplemented from the left operand makes Python try the reflected method on the right (__rmul__, __radd__)
sum() starts from 0, so it needs __radd__ (or a start value)
a closure is a function that keeps the variables of the call that made it, so _backward can be stored and run later
build_topo appends a node after its inputs; reversed, that is the backprop order

retrieve.q: Explain why the r methods exist at all: what situation would be impossible to handle if Python only ever called the left operand's method?
answer: a built-in type on the left (an int) can't know about your class
so the right operand needs a way to take over
Python calls it only after the left one returns NotImplemented

retrieve.q: Walk through sum([m1, m2, m1]) call by call, naming each dunder method that runs and the Money it produces.
answer: then __add__ with m2 → 350, and with m1 → Money(cents=600)

retrieve.q: Trace build_topo(L) on L = d·f, d = e + c, e = a·b (inputs visited in the order written). What list comes out, and why is L last?
answer: a, b, e, c, d, f, L
each node is appended only after all its inputs have been appended
L depends on everything, so it's last; reversed, it's first to run _backward

retrieve.q: micrograd stores one closure per result instead of one central backward function that switches on _op. What do you gain, and what does it cost?
answer: gain: each op's derivative sits next to its forward code; adding an op touches one place
cost: one function object per node, and the backward logic is scattered across methods
cost: a bug like out._backward = _backward() (storing the call's None) only shows up later, when backprop calls it

compare.q: Money and Value both overload + and *. What does Value store on each result that Money doesn't, and why does that one difference turn arithmetic into a computation graph?
answer: both create a new object inside __add__/__mul__
Value also stores its parents (_prev) and the op (_op), later a _backward closure
Money forgets where its cents came from, so there's nothing to walk back through

compare.q: This card's build_topo runs on a dict of names; that card runs it on real Values. What changes when the inputs come from a set (_prev) instead of a list, and what stays guaranteed?
answer: siblings (like a and b) can come out in a different order between runs
still guaranteed: every node after all its inputs
so backprop gives the same gradients whatever the sibling order

predict.q: Delete the visited set from micrograd's build_topo, then run backward() on x = a·b, y = x + 1, z = x·2, L = y·z with a = 2, b = −3. The correct a.grad is 66. What do you get, and why?
predict.answer: Wrong answers: 96 or 102 depending on the set order (computed; x.grad is still −22). x feeds both y and z, so without visited it lands in the topo list twice, and its _backward runs twice, adding its gradient into a and b a second time, once before x's gradient is even complete. visited is what makes each node run exactly once.

apply.task: Give your Money class subtraction without any new arithmetic, the way micrograd's engine.py does: __neg__ as self * -1, __sub__ as self + (-other), and __rsub__ as other + (-self). Then print -m1, m1 - m2 and 1000 - m1 with m1 = Money(250), m2 = Money(100).
apply.done: You see Money(cents=-250), Money(cents=150) and Money(cents=750), and you can say which of your methods ran for 1000 - m1 (int gives up, so __rsub__).
apply.hint: 1000 - m1 reaches m1.__rsub__(1000), which computes 1000 + (-m1), and that in turn needs __radd__.
